readerTitle: Your friend's startup grew almost 4x. Read the numbers before you invest.
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (앱으로 주간 식단을 파는 밀프렙 스타트업) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 매출 성장이라는 헤드라인 하나가 아니라 손익계산서, 현금흐름표, 재무상태표를 차례로 읽어야 사업의 실제 모습이 보인다.
misconception: 매출이 빠르게 늘고 통장에 돈이 있으면 사업은 괜찮다.

sources.text: 재무회계의 표준 개념 (손익계산서, 현금흐름표, 재무상태표, 매출총이익률과 순이익률)

factChecks.note: 현금: 순손실 $3,000 + 장비 구입 $9,000 = 현금 감소 $12,000. 단순화를 위해 감가상각과 기타 운전자본 변동은 무시했습니다.
투자 여부에 대한 법률·세무 조언이 아니라 재무제표 읽기 연습으로만 다룹니다.

cards.title: Your friend's startup grew almost 4x. Read the numbers before you invest.
body: Your friend Dana runs a meal-prep startup. She cooks healthy lunches in a rented kitchen and sells weekly plans through her own app.
She asks you to invest $20,000. Her pitch has one big number: monthly revenue up from $8,000 to $30,000 in six months. You have four questions to ask. Choose well.

image.label: A pitch slide with a steep revenue line next to lunch boxes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 주방 테이블 위에 도시락 상자들과 노트북. 노트북 화면에 가파르게 오르는 매출 그래프와 "$8,000 → $30,000" 문구. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you ask first?
body: Revenue is clearly growing. Dana is excited and wants an answer this week.

options.text: How fast can it keep growing?
options.feedback: You hear an exciting forecast, but you still don't know if each sale makes or loses money. Growth multiplies whatever is underneath it.

options.text: What's left after costs? Show me last month's income statement.
options.feedback: Revenue is what customers pay. Profit is what stays. Asking for the income statement turns one headline into the full story of the month.

options.text: How many people downloaded the app?
options.feedback: Downloads show interest, not money. Useful later, but they can rise while the business loses more.

cards.title: The margin is shrinking.
body: Say you chose B. Last month: revenue $30,000. Food, packaging and delivery $18,000, so **gross profit** is $12,000, or 40%. Rent, staff, app and marketing cost $15,000. Net loss: $3,000.
Dana adds: "Six months ago our gross margin was 50%. Bigger volume will fix the loss." What do you ask?

options.text: Fair. More orders spread the rent and staff costs
options.feedback: Rent does spread out. But if each order keeps leaving less, more orders won't close the gap as fast as she hopes.

options.text: Why does each order leave less than it used to?
options.feedback: She admits growth came from free delivery on every plan. Food costs haven't changed, but delivery now eats a bigger slice. Part of the growth was bought with margin.

options.text: Cut marketing so the next month shows a profit
options.feedback: The loss vanishes on paper for a month, and so does the growth. The shrinking margin is still there.

cards.title: The bank fell faster than the loss.
body: Say you chose B. Dana plans to charge for delivery on small orders. Next you look at the bank.
The loss last month was $3,000. But the bank balance fell by $12,000. What explains the gap?

options.text: Something is being hidden. Walk away
options.feedback: Big gaps deserve questions, not panic. You'd lose a possibly good deal over an answer that was easy to find.

options.text: Open the cash flow statement and find spending missing from the income statement
options.feedback: It shows $9,000 for a second oven and a used van. Equipment counts as an asset, so its cost hits profit slowly over years. The cash left all at once.
A common cause in many businesses, but Dana's customers prepay in the app. Checking the statement beats guessing.

cards.title: How long will the money last?
body: Say you chose B. Dana says: "We have $25,000 in the bank. At a $3,000 monthly loss, that's eight months."
The **balance sheet** also lists $6,000 owed to suppliers this month and an $8,000 loan payment due in two months.

options.text: About eight months, as she says
options.feedback: That treats all $25,000 as free. $14,000 of it is already promised to others, so the business could run short much sooner.

options.text: Under four months, after the bills already owed
options.feedback: $25,000 − $6,000 − $8,000 leaves $11,000. At $3,000 a month, that's under four months. Your $20,000 would buy time, not a cushion.
You counted the supplier bill but not the loan. Closer, but still too hopeful.

cards.title: One headline, three statements.

breakdown.label: Cash change
breakdown.detail: Cash flow statement: includes $9,000 of equipment

cards.softwareNote: A software startup reads the same way: gross margin after hosting and support, cash spent on yearly tool contracts, and customers' prepaid annual plans sitting on the balance sheet as money not yet earned.

cards.title: One month is only a snapshot.
body: Equipment is bought in lumps, so a single month can look worse, or better, than the trend. Ask for six to twelve months side by side.
Early statements are often put together by the founder, not checked by an accountant. Ask how the numbers were made before trusting them.
And runway math assumes nothing changes. A price rise or a new loss changes it fast.

cards.title: Growth is the headline. The three statements are the story.
body: Each question you asked used a different part of this unit:
list: **Decision 1:** revenue vs profit, read on the income statement
**Decision 2:** gross vs net margin, and why each sale matters
**Decision 3:** the cash flow statement, where equipment shows up
**Decision 4:** the balance sheet, where money already owed hides
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take your own last month. Write revenue, net profit, the change in your bank balance, and what you already owe. Do the four tell the same story?
